display.title: Tanya Shiur 33a: Tanya Chapter 17, "Ki Karov Eilecha HaDavar Meod"
display.summary_short: A Yiddish Tanya shiur on chapter 17: why the verse 'the thing is very near to you' is the foundation of Tanya, and how the mind can bring love of Hashem into action.
display.summary_long: Shiur 33a in Rabbi Yosef Goldstein's Yiddish Tanya series, given on Rosh Chodesh Kislev 5737. After a short review of the beinoni's service in chapter 16, the class opens chapter 17. The Alter Rebbe built the whole Tanya on the verse 'For the thing is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, to do it', one of the Twelve Pesukim; the first sixteen chapters prepare the way to understand it. The shiur explains the order of mouth, heart and action, and why the word 'to do it' takes a different letter: everything must lead to actual deeds. How can the heart be called near, when only tzaddikim rule their hearts? The answer is that the mind is in a person's control. By thinking about the greatness of Hashem, anyone can reach the love that brings him to do mitzvos. Along the way: guarding the eyes, the place of the nigun in Chabad, and the Mitteler Rebbe on how love can be commanded. For one who has fallen low, the path is teshuvah first, with a broken heart that breaks through the barrier of sin. Stories illustrate saying the words of Tehillim clearly. The class ends with a hope for Moshiach and a short story about the Baal Shem Tov.
display.lesson: Love of Hashem that leads to action is within everyone's reach, because the mind can rule the heart; even one who has fallen can return through teshuvah.

date.note: The speaker says it is now Rosh Chodesh Kislev 5737 and that Hallel was said today.

segments.title: Ch. 17: the verse on which Tanya is founded
Mouth, heart and action: why 'to do it' comes last
Is the heart near? Tzaddikim rule their hearts
The mind rules the heart: love that leads to action
Meditation and the nigun in Chabad
The Mitteler Rebbe: how love can be commanded
The purpose of man: action in this world
One who has fallen low: teshuvah first, with a broken heart
Saying the words of Tehillim clearly: polished coins and a limping angel
Breaking through the barrier; weeping at night, joy in the morning
Closing story: the Baal Shem Tov's shoes and a blessing
